newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Fight for CA heats up as deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Fight for CA heats up as deadline looms.

text.p: Political infighting over the sale of Austria's Creditanstalt heated up on Wednesday as bidders convened for hectic last-minute negotiations to put the final touches to their rival offers for the country's number two bank.

A disillusioned group of suitors led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali met behind closed doors to ponder whether they could top up their existing bid for Creditanstalt, which is three billion schillings ($270 million) short of a competing offer by Bank Austria.
No information on the outcome of the talks could be expected before Friday, a spokesman for the group told Reuters.
"We just can't say anything," he said.
Market leader Bank Austria's supervisory board was called to a special meeting on Thursday to review its own bid, one day before Finance Minister Viktor Klima's final deadline for adjusted offers.

The debate over what has become Europe's longest-running privatisation battle plunged into increasingly murky waters on Wednesday with leaders of Austria's creaky government coalition publicly exchanging jibes over the hotly-contested sell-off.

Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, whose Social Democrats strongly back Bank Austria's bid, warned his party would not be bullied into a decision by their junior coalition partner, the People's Party of Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel.

The conservatives, who fear losing control of blue-blooded Creditanstalt and support the bid by EA-Generali, have called for a special session of parliament on Tuesday to discuss the sale. Senior members of both parties will meet in emergency talks on Monday.

Schuessel's attempt to appease his angered coalition partner by suggesting that Bank Austria might buy half of the state's Creditanstalt stake with the rest being floated on the stock exchange was flatly rejected by Vranitzky.
"This is a bad option...the law dictates that we sell to the highest bidder," the chancellor said.
EA-Generali's chances of getting its hands on the bank have faded since Bank Austria entered the seven-year race for the state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt last month.
Bank Austria, controlled by the Social Democratic-dominated City of Vienna council through its Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse, has bid 16.8 billion schillings for the bank.

EA-Generali and its co-bidders, among them savings bank Die Erste, Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commercialie Italiana, have offered a total of 13.8 billion schillings for the state's 19.9 million shares in the bank and want to sell about a quarter of those on the market.

But the assortment of international financial and industrial interests last week signalled it would be hard pressed to match Bank Austria's bid, saying they had all but given up hope of getting their hands on the country's most traditional bank.

If the consortium fails to outbid Bank Austria, the Social Democrats have left little doubt that a merger of the country's two top banks is all but a done deal, raising the spectre of a major shakeup in Austria's overcrowded banking system.

"A decision must swiftly be made after the 10th for the best bidder and the highest offer," Vranitzky said, in apparent defiance of the conservative's repeated warning that no decision must be made before Tuesday's parliament session. ($1=11.05 Schilling)
